newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO talks frozen, U.S. envoy returns home.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO talks frozen, U.S. envoy returns home.

text.p: U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross failed to break a two-month deadlock in Israeli-Palestinian peace talks before heading home on Saturday.
"I think what is important as I leave the region is that there is a very clear desire to find a way out... to find a way to promote moving towards peace," Ross said before departing Israel.
Ross held separate meetings with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on Friday in a final bid to bridge the gaps between the sides.
But the sides refused to budge from positions which froze on March 18 when Israel broke ground on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.
Arafat, disappointed by the Ross mission, called on the U.S. to take a more active role in its mediation, PLO officials said.
"Arafat told Ross that a greater American role is the only way out of the crisis," said Arafat adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah.

All Ross had to show for his nine-day mission was a meeting between Israeli and PLO security chiefs that Israel denounced as insufficient and a second meeting between high-level officials from the sides which Palestinians derided as a failure.
"I will be reporting back to the president (Bill Clinton) and the secretary (Madeleine Albright) on how to best work with the parties to move ahead and to try to proceed," Ross said.
"We will continue to be facilitating contact between the parties because we know the best way to move forward is for all of us to work together," the American envoy added.
The Palestinians demand Israel halt all settlement activity, which they see as an attempt to pre-empt final peace talks, as a condition to resuming negotiations.
Israel, which has accused the Palestinian Authority of creating an "artificial crisis" in negotiations, has linked a renewal of talks with a PLO crackdown on "terror".
"There is an attempt, apparently by the Palestinian Authority, by its leader, to create an artificial crisis," said Israeli Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh on Friday.
Arafat sent a letter to Clinton complaining indirectly at Ross's performance and asking the U.S. president to personally step in to salvage the process.

"Arafat informed Ross that he is not happy with the American mediation role and the Israeli delaying tactics. That is why he sent the letter to President Clinton asking him to intervene personally to resolve the crisis," Abu Rdainah said.
In Washington, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told visiting Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy that the U.S. could provide only limited help to move the process forward.
Albright also made it clear that she was not prepared to visit the region until the parties made "difficult decisions" required to overcome the current impasse.
